title: To the Child Alfredo H. and R.
text:
Beside the mother's bridal bed

a tender cradle sways,

the two loving spouses

invoke fortune

with celestial affection

for the sleeping child:

he dreams of the angels

he has just left.


The child's soft ecstasy

is seen in the tender face;

a loving, candid vow

is painted on the mother's;

on the father's somber face,

a pious thought…

May benevolent God

wish to hear their vows!


Her mystical vow

holds the sweetest wish:

to give, like a heavenly god,

an angel to the earth;

the father's thought

is violently stirred:

that a man, through his love,

has been given to the wretched world.


To the valley of tears,

be welcome, Alfredo,

where, without dreadful thorns,

as in a flower garden,

life may smile on you,

and the sun of joy

may always shine clear for you

without clouds of sorrow.


I do not want the poet's

sad, untamed genius

to inspire you,

the genius that clouds

his restless soul;

the power that inspires his lyre

with sacred fire

to drape his heart in bitterest grief.


I do not want glory's splendor,

though it be magnificent,

to drag you down a harsh path

after posthumous remembrance;

so dazzling a diadem

burns the ardent brow,

and it is a horrible, dropsical

thirst for ambition.


May the magical gleam

of riches not entice you;

for sordid greed

tarnishes and darkens

the soul's beauty,

and in it does not flower

the tree that gives life

to sweet charity.


May heaven free you from

that lethal wisdom

which gives genius

a sacrilegious altar of idolatry;

it does not see in man

a brother's heart,

and worships the idol

of vainglorious pride.


And if the peaceful path

of your precious life

by harsh brambles

should be obstructed;

may your pure soul become

like steel in hardship,

and may it firmly, fearlessly

challenge the struggle.


Do not shine like a Socrates

or a Redeemer Messiah

if the age of martyrs

is no longer granted to your days;

splendid and divine

was their destiny,

but sad it is on a Golgotha

to die… and not to save.


May your learning be worthy,

sweet child, and magnanimous;

may it shine, without twilight,

your ermine heart;

may thought not dry up

the flower of feeling,

and may sorrowful man inspire you

with love and compassion.


And when swift time,

after a pure existence,

carries you to the barren realm

of the dark region,

may family, homeland, and man

give laurels to your name,

and the archangels cry:

“Alfredo, blessing!”
editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem’s extended benediction and its alternating maternal and paternal wishes; a slightly elliptical source phrase about the father’s “somber” face is kept as an image.

title: Fierce Love
text:
Oh, fierce love, you came like the butterfly

that approaches the rose when October begins;

everything was silence, open silence

to mysterious shadows like a dead man's eye.


I was the same shadow, I was less, I was

a sleeping thing that neither dreams nor hopes,

when the flight of that celestial butterfly

suddenly made me warble like a wild bird.


Oh, a hundred suns rose in the east,

oh, a hundred rivers ran down the same slope,

oh, a hundred silver moons shone in the sky,

and a hundred high mountains took flight.


I opened my arms: I had the divine madness

of touching the things of the heights with my fingers.

I opened my eyes: I had the divine sadness

of drinking celestial beauty with my eyes.


I wept, I wept without cease; I cried: My heart,

stop on the road that leads to delirium;

but my heart was a drop of wax...

God, what could that drop do against spring?...


Fierce love: into your hands I have released my life;

receive it: a Dove that settles, exhausted,

in bloodstained claws no longer beats its wings:

it dies from what it lives on; it lives from what you exhale.


I know well that no hundred suns are born in the east,

I know well that no hundred rivers run down one slope,

I know well that no hundred moons shine in the sky,

I know well that no mountains lengthen into flight.


I know well that doves blind their eyes, leave

their feathers in the nest, and dawns draw away,

leaves fall, autumn comes, death,

days turn gray, and fortune turns gray.


But I am a slave to pain and adore it

as the miser adores the sound of gold:

oh, terrible storm of lightning and thunder,

in your fire I revive, in your fire I faint.


Fierce love: I am small as a snowflake,

fierce love: I am small as a little bird,

sad as the moan of a dying child,

fierce love, you would find no better prey in the world.


No one would die more lightly in your claws,

no one would die sooner in your bonds.

Shine, rising sun... Nature, grow:

over dark life, death shines.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the poem’s deliberate multiplication of suns, rivers, moons, and mountains, then returns to ordinary seasonal mortality.

title: Caravan
text:
Today we had word of the poet:

amid the lullaby of mouth organs

and with the arms of the last stars hanging down,

he halted his horse.


The women's camp clapped its hands,

seasoning the corn tortillas.

The girls bit the stems of flowers,

and the old men sealed tearful friendships

amid the libations of the deep dawn.


They carried basins of water,

and the chief prepared

to wash his chest, his head, and his beard.


The potters of the seven wives

were already caressing the damp jars.

The children of the country that does nothing

lit cigarettes as long as sticks.


And in the morning sacrifice,

lambs for everyone

turned, skewered on pikes,

over the blaze of fragrant logs.


Today we had word of the poet,

because he was asleep on horseback.

He said they carry God upon their horns

and that the night has acid roses

on the carpets of the two twilights.
editorial_note: The translation retains the poem’s surreal caravan ritual, including its deliberately strange social and sacrificial images.

title: The Ominous Sign
text:
I


If they tell you I am growing old

because reading tires me

or the pen wearies me, or I have had enough

of philosophies I do not understand;


if another judges that I collect the dividend

from an invested treasure, and claims

that I live on my own sinecure

and depend only on my habits,


send them to the new spring

that must bring forth shoots, so that

they may forget yesterday's fruits;


but if you know that I closed my eyes

to the challenge of red lips,

then you may count me lost.


II


Without forgetting for a moment

the patience and resignation of the gardener,

at every hour I apply the diligence

my daily commerce requires.


Since I have never felt the difference

between what I lose and what I gain,

I sow without slackness or fervor

in the furrow traced by my hand.


While the appointed hour arrives,

I guard the bud, tend the graft,

raise the stem of the beloved flower,


pull the weeds from my garden,

and when I loosen my fist from the hoe

you will pronounce me dead without asking.
editorial_note: The two sonnet-like sections preserve the poem’s shift from rumors of aging to the gardening metaphor of desire and death.

title: To Cuernavaca!
text:
I


To Cuernavaca I go, sweet retreat,

when, through whim or discouragement,

I yield to the desire to interrupt the tale

and give my story some breathing room.


To Cuernavaca I go, asking only

to enjoy its airs for a moment:

a pause of freedom and recreation

a sigh's brief distance away.


Neither country nor city, summit nor hollow;

beatific solitude, quiet that soothes,

or gentle company without surfeit.


Vegetal warmth in which being rocks

in philosophical measure...

To Cuernavaca I go, to Cuernavaca!


II


I do not know whether I inspire it with my mood

or whether repose is granted me by design.

Whether reality or pretense,

why do I ask myself, why do I rave?


It is enough for me to know, sweet retreat,

that you soothe my temples with your breath:

a pause of freedom and recreation

a sigh's brief distance away.


The quiet and the light the soul drinks

like cordial wine; the magpie trills,

and the laurel murmurs of birds;


a cloud flies; a star stands out,

and time itself suspends and lasts...

To Cuernavaca I go, to Cuernavaca!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the repeated destination refrain and the poem’s balanced contrast between retreat, freedom, quiet, and light.

title: Gloss of My Land
text:
I


Let the red carnation sleep

or the white jasmine of the temples;

for the thistle is only disdain,

and the laurel only fury.

Let the altar boy give his honey,

and the wrinkled orange

and the thirsty pomegranate

juice and blood—gold and ruby;

for I prefer you to them,

little purple poppy.



II


At the foot of the leafy fig tree

the little carpet spreads its mantle;

the simple anacua grows,

and the courtly rose;

where the butterfly does not,

the hummingbird turns it iridescent.

But I prefer you,

whose hand draws away:

vessel in which sleeps the lament

of the valley where I was born.



III


When day is reborn

and the siesta awakens,

the magpies celebrate

with salvos of clamor,

why, poppy, so cold,

or so pure, or so silent?

Why, without telling me anything,

do you fill me with an uncertain longing—

an exhausted cup, an open hand—

if you are not in love?



IV


Will golden stars be born

from your trembling chalice—

a rule for thought

or a little box for tears?

No sonorous song is worth

the silence I heard from you.

I am testing in you

how much music errs.

Poppy of my land:

fall in love with me.
editorial_note: “Anacua,” “bujeta,” and the local flowers are retained or rendered cautiously; “bujeta” is translated as a small box while preserving the source’s uncertainty.

title: To Die
text:
On the most loving bed
I feel myself dying,
when in nature,
all is as gentle as a garden.


Soft, the white angel's wing
—what pity, what tenderness at last!—
for the first time brushes my shoulders
as a bow brushes a violin.


This freshness of knowing
that we too are leaving here,
what novelty in consciousness,
what soft and subtle persuasion!


What acceptance, what smoothness,
what letting oneself go!
Their edges and points, the acts
round off as they reach me.


Neither the stoic's bloodletting,
who diminished without feeling,
nor the asp that barely kissed
the bud of anxious crimson:


A slow decline, and so sure—
swollen with itself—
that it leaves no room for laments
or fears, nor


even the vague tickle
of that minute to come
in which something that must open
will open before my eyes.


How natural what ends
when it ends by itself!
I go with reason satisfied,
asleep, content, happy.


And I, who lived so many years,
so many years that I lost,
without listening to the sphinx
that whispered beside me!


I did not know that life reclines
and holds itself thus
in that greed of nothingness
which is its divan, its cushion.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem’s gentle acceptance of death, including the unfinished “nor” and the final image of nothingness as furniture.

title: Monterrey Sun
text:
There is no doubt: as a child,
the sun followed me.


It walked behind me
like a lapdog;
disheveled and sweet,
bright and yellow:
that sleepy sun
that follows children.


It leaped from patio to patio,
rolled about in my bedroom.
I still believe that sometimes
they chased it away with a broom.
And the next morning,
it was with me again,
disheveled and sweet,
bright and yellow:
that sleepy sun
that follows children.


(The fire of May
knighted me:
I was the Wandering Child,
and the sun, my squire.)


All the sky was indigo;
the whole house was gold.
How much sun entered me
through my eyes!
A sea deep inside my forehead,
wherever I go,
even when clouds are closed,
oh, how much the sun weighs on me!
Oh, how it aches inside,
that cistern of sun
that travels with me!


In my childhood I knew
no shade, only sun-glare.
Every window was sun,
every room was windows.


The corridors stretched
arches of light through the house.
In the trees the embers
of oranges burned,
and the orchard in living flame
turned golden.
The peacocks were
kin to the sun. The heron
began to flame
at every step it took.


And the sun undressed me
to cling to me,
disheveled and sweet,
bright and yellow:
that sleepy sun
that follows children.


When I left my house
with my cane and bundle,
I said to my heart:
“You have sun enough for a while!”
It is treasure—and it does not end:
it does not end—I spend it.
I carry so much sun inside
that so much sun now tires me.
In my childhood I knew
no shade, only sun-glare.
editorial_note: “Resolana” is rendered as “sun-glare,” keeping the poem’s distinction between shade and the intense reflected heat of childhood.

title: The Tune of the Enemy Servant
text:
Deaf little song, sad,
discordant song;
song trilled sotto voce
and stolen from labor,
behind the mistress's back;
at the master's patience;
deaf little song, sad,
slave song, song,
song of a young slave girl who feels
memory is treacherous;
song of filing chains
beneath its murmur;
song of outpourings
drowned in fear;
song of a slave that tastes
of forbidden fruit:
—you appear to me wholly
in two eyes and a voice.


Between her teeth, barely heard,
words of rebellion:
“War on another's fortune,
war on another's pain!
Sweep their house, wind,
for I will not sweep it.
Spin them the fleece, spider,
for I will not spin it.
San Telmo, light the sails,
San Pascual, tend the hearth.
Today the needle pricked me
and the spindle broke;
and such is the tyranny
of this dissimulation,
that though rare longings
swell my heart,
I have looks of defiance
and a voice of resignation.”


Fierce were her eyes,
and hoarse and mild her voice;
refined imaginings
and a plebeian heart.
Her mother, being simple,
did not know how to marry her, no.
A witness to other lives,
her spirit betrays her.
Deaf little song, sad,
slave song, song:
—you appear to me wholly
in two eyes and a voice.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the servant’s covert song, named saints, household labor, and the tension between rebellious eyes and a resigned voice.

title: The Bad Confectioner
text:
Toledo is an ecclesiastical city.

For a single night of the year,

its household vines

give a clear wine.


A little wine that reddens the palate

of the eponymous marzipan,

and very gently prepares one

to receive into the soul the canonical aroma

of black grapes in brandy.


For the Church

allows gluttony:

for every craving there is a license;

for every sweet, a papal bull.


And candid sugar drips

through the transparency of the Cathedral;

and in her arms the Virgin cradles

the little edible god,

pink and salmon;

and oh, what famous slices of the Alcázar,

if, being granite, they were nougat!


For the Church allows gluttony;

and I know a nun who is all sugar.

And who keeps heaven addicted

to honey spun through her hair,

and knows how to make walnut electuaries,

and others of bitter-root carrots,

and citron, codonate, and rosetta,

and Alexandrian cumin sweet,

and so many other things I could not finish.


But that confectioner—where was he—

who made the holy mysteries

in sugar, almond, and cinnamon?

Pentecost and the Trinity,

Corpus and the Ascension,

and a Jesus almost true

with a little almond in his heart.


But art has its rules,

and each figure its share.

And there was also a Lucifer

with a sour, elongated face,

and he put in his heart

an unusual bitter almond.


Terror of mothers: hidden death

in the sweets!

Seasoning by the handful,

with the verdigris of kitchens!


I know well that art has its rules,

and each figure gets its share.

But to sugar-coat bitter almonds,

even if they are the heart's?

Unneeded charities,

I swear they are.


To disguise a Lucifer cunningly,

so that he is mistaken for a Savior?

Unneeded charities,

I swear they are.


Oh, good maker!

There is better art:

do not sell me rancor in syrup,

if I am to find gall

in the heart.
editorial_note: The source contains the marked phrase “aroma Canonical”; it is retained as “canonical aroma” rather than silently normalized. Rare confection names are transliterated or rendered descriptively.

title: The Creole Woman's Eyes
text:
Sometimes they are clear, and sometimes wheat-colored

like earth burned by the sun's fire...

The Creole woman whose lips carry a faint flush

and whose dark eyes carry a dreaming soul...


When the strings of a sad guitar weep,

her eyes are dyed the color of illusion,

and from her warm breast her heart departs,

when the strings of a sad guitar weep...


In the pale hours of moonlit nights,

beneath the discreet canopy of the shadowy amate,

her eyes reflect like the ripples of a river

in the pale hours of moonlit nights...


When she goes on Sundays to the nearby church,

with her dark, olive-colored eyes,

compliments follow her and love importunes her,

when she goes on Sundays to the nearby church...


When the strings of a sweet guitar weep,

in the pale hours of moonlit nights,

her olive-colored eyes grow sad,

when the strings of a sweet guitar weep.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem’s refrain structure and its local images of the amate tree, olive-colored eyes, and guitars.

title: Pueblan Airs
text:
I do not know what suggestive graces

these villages of white little houses possess,

full of groves, full of ravines,

and fresh girls who rise early.


Quiet little villages, where the bell

of the old church sings for joy

when, beyond the mountain ridges,

the blushing morning laughs...


I do not know what innocent graces

these peaceful, quiet villages possess,

where grandmothers lull their grandchildren

inside the hammocks of the corridors...


Sweet little villages where cicadas

sing on the clear days of April,

while, by the fire of loving logs,

trembling guitars keep their tunes...


Peaceful corners where existence

runs gently, like pure water;

where even the winds, full of freshness,

carry notes of innocence on their wings...


I do not know what suggestive charms

these villages, soft as a nest, possess,

where sweet forgetfulness, sweet forgetfulness,

lays a rose-colored mantle over sorrows...
editorial_note: The repeated village descriptions and refrain are preserved, with “pueblos” rendered variously as villages or little towns to retain the poem’s tender scale.

title: Raft of Flowers
text:
That hamlet had a special way

of being:

the air fresher, cleaner, and everything,

everything was a landscape painted on glass!


For being soft and sweet, for being plaintive,

the birds' voices were almost a sigh...

And blue was the distant sierra, as though one saw it

behind a sapphire...


For the sadness of those paths,

the fragrant flowers had words;

and in the tamarind trees, with the clarineros,

zenzontles moaned, turtledoves wept...


The sun-gilded tile-roofed ranches

rose rough among the murmuring green of the cane,

and the lemon trees gave their velvet shadows

to the open balcony facing the mountains.


And you were the aloof, brown Pueblan girl;

and I was the traveler full of illusion;

and when you appeared, how lovely the happy morning became,

as if roses were springing from the balcony!...


And your loves were a raft of flowers,

brown girl, Pueblan girl, honey of the cane fields...

And my love was the water that wept in torrents

so the raft of flowers might float...
editorial_note: “Clarineros” and “zenzontles” are retained as local bird names; the translation keeps the poem’s final water-and-flowers metaphor.

title: This Was a Wing
text:
She always rewarded my visit

with the gold of an enchanting tale;

innocence lived in the little old woman

as sky water lives in a flower...


She adored children and blue;

she was always dressed in innocence,

and the clothes she kept in the trunk

smelled of basil and camphor...


How early-rising she and the doves were:

because the courtyard was covered in flowers,

it almost always dawned

beneath the trees, sweeping aromas...


And at night, in the lamplight,

she prayed with such deep devotion

that the moon, appearing at the balcony,

found her soul in the breviary.


One night among so many... alas, my friend

did not appear at the corridor again.

“She is ill,” they said: “a pain,

a weariness, a silence, a fatigue”...


The doctor came and began prescribing,

murmuring in a low voice: “She is very ill”...

And I learned the sad story: this was a wing,

tired of flying...


And did she leave? Like everything; four candles

filled the little room with sadness.

How that saintly whiteness of her head

was confused with the lilies!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the old woman’s devotional tenderness and the final wing metaphor, allowing “candor” to become the more idiomatic “innocence.”

title: Native Orchards
text:
Beneath awnings of blond orange groves

the dusty road winds,

full of aromas and wind,

full of spring music.


At the first morning light

the cattle pass with their slow gait...

and the farmhand follows behind, dirty and begrimed,

riding his colt to the corrals.


Beside the old door he milks the udder,

and the fragrant, foaming milk

bubbles in the overflowing jar.

And the sun, in its local caress,

kindles the orange grove, fresh and sonorous,

as though it were throwing handfuls of gold...


Among the green foliage, the cabin

shows its rustic, thatched roof.

Beside it stands the golden-reed bamboo

creaking amid the tangled green.


In the distance the flexible cane rocks

its high plume, curled by the wind,

and as it undulates, its solid reed

raises the murmur of a strange song.


Amid so much beauty, nevertheless,

nothing inspires the soul with more sweetness

than that emerald distance,

embroidered with virgin thicket...

a hill rises there, and on its slope

a coconut palm waves its fan...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the rural vocabulary, local vegetation, and the closing emerald distance and coconut palm; “la ubre ordeña” is rendered as the ordinary milking scene its syntax implies.

title: Let Us Sing Our Own
text:
What a charm life has, if native winds

on their light wings bring lost echoes

of stream music and nest music,

like gentle preludes from soft instruments!


What a charm life has, if beneath the bohío's shelter,

amid an intense fragrance of lilies and basil,

we look at the corrals where the cows low

and hear the stanzas of the murmuring river!...


The soil is the source of inspiration:

why seek happiness in foreign lands,

if we have Decembers thick with stars,

if we have Octobers pregnant with illusions!


Not from the Pagan Mount does the inspiring muse descend

to the estates of pale poets:

our native muse lives in the arbors of purple and mother-of-pearl,

where dawn dies.


It is our Indian muse who, from her cabin,

descends crowned with quetzal feathers

to inspire simple, tender madrigals,

fragrant with forest and mountain flowers.


Come, then, let us dream beneath warm eaves

of flowering orange trees, beside the springs:

October gives us its roses and evening blooms;

December the myriads of all its stars.
editorial_note: The source’s “silos natales vientos” is read as the evident “si los natales vientos” (“if native winds”); the translation preserves the native muse and seasonal imagery.

title: My Mother's Hands
text:
Hands like my mother's, so caressing,

so silken, so entirely hers, white and beneficent.

They alone are holy, they alone are the ones who love,

the ones who lavish everything and ask nothing of me!

Those that, to relieve me of doubts and quarrels,

draw out my thorns and drive them into themselves!


For the bitter heat of hidden sorrows,

nothing compares with the coolness of those two lilies.

When life leaves my flowers withered,

they are two white miracles soothing anguish!

And when the evils of fate hound me,

they are two wings of peace over my storms.


They are celestial, miraculous hands,

because they make stars bloom in my shadow.

For pain, caresses; for sorrow, unction;

they are the only hands that have a heart!

(Rosebush of everlasting white roses:

learn whiteness from maternal hands.)


I, who carry hidden doubts in my soul,

when the wings of illusion have fallen,

my mother's hands upon my breast are

like two quiet wings over my heart!

My mother's hands know how to erase sadness!

My mother's hands perfume everything with tenderness!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the repeated anaphora and the poem’s transformation of maternal hands into lilies, wings, stars, and a rosebush.

title: The Eyes of Oxen
text:
I have seen them so sad that I can hardly think

how, being so sad, they can never weep!...


And they are always so: whether afternoon

kisses them with kisses of soft flushes,

or clear night looks at them with its suns,

or joyful foliage shelters them with its shade...


Whether climbing the slope that leads to the hamlet,

among glaucous rows of coffee trees in bloom...

or watching the waters of some murmuring

little stream running beneath a shadowy forest...


What can those eyes have, always dreaming

and always open?...

Always moist and vague and shadowy and uncertain,

as though they were always silently imploring!


Once, on the path of a flowering grotto,

I saw a solitary ox gazing at the ground

with long insistence, as though in its longings

it were anxiously seeking its lost freedom...


And again beneath a tree and beside the cart

loaded with bundles, and later in the depths

of a clear ravine, and on the immense plain,

and in a purple-and-violet sunset...


Always sad and vague, the eyes of those kings

who are now slaves! I cannot think

how, being so sad, they can never weep—

the eyes of oxen...
editorial_note: The translation retains the oxen as fallen kings and preserves the poem’s repeated question about eyes that are sorrowful yet cannot weep.

title: Ascension
text:
Two wings!... Who might have two wings for flight?
This afternoon, on the summit, I almost had them.
From here I see the sea, so blue, so asleep,
that if it were not a sea, it would surely be another sky!...


Divine summits, exalted lookouts!
How small men are! No rumors reach us
from down there, from the mire; nor the horrifying cry
with which desire howls, nor the overflowing clamor
of evil passions... The lowly does not rise:
this summit is the kingdom of the bird and the cloud...


Here I saw something very sweet and strange:
it was like seeing a mountain weep...
the water rises slowly, and light shines in its pool;
a little calf comes, then kneels
at the edge of the pond, and lowering its head,
to drink clean water, drinks water and light...


And then a sound is heard through hill and forest,
as if a storm were rolling down the slope:
animals come, seized by a strange fever,
to drink the tears the mountain weeps.


Night is approaching. The sea can no longer be seen.
And what disgust, what sadness, to begin descending...


(Who might have two wings, two wings for a flight?
This afternoon, on the summit, I almost had them,
with the mad desire to have spread them
over that sleeping sea that looked like a sky!)


A river amid greenery is lost behind me,
like a silver thread threading emeralds...
editorial_note: The translation preserves the ascent and descent, the mountain’s tears, and the final sea-as-sky image; lineation follows the source’s stanza skeleton.

title: The Return
text:
“Living without your caresses is great desolation;
living without your words is great solitude;
living without your loving gaze, ingenuous and clear,
is great darkness…”


I return, pale bride, whom you used to await
my return so early in the morning,
with the same song you preferred
and the same tenderness of other days
and the same love as always, to your window.


And I choose to see you, in delicate
complicity with Nature,
an afternoon like this: fainting
on a bed of lilacs, and imbued
with a certain aristocratic sadness.


I return to you with fingers intertwined
in an attitude of supplication and yearning
—as always—and lips untired
of praising you, and eyes obstinate
in seeing yours through the sky!


Receive me calmly, without rancor,
showing the soft manner of a sister;
murmur a peaceful “I forgive you,”
and let me sleep in abandon,
in your noble lap, until tomorrow….
